description: Hi, I’m Siddartha. I’m a Master’s student in Computer Science at the University of Cincinnati and a software engineer intern at DXC Technology, and before that I worked as a software engineer at TCS. I build full-stack and data products, mostly in Python, FastAPI, React/TypeScript, PostgreSQL and scikit-learn, and I deploy them with Docker and AWS.
summary:
FieldWise gives an Ohio farmer one date: the last day they can still plant a cover crop or winter wheat on their own field.

Bare winter fields wash soil and fertilizer into Lake Erie. Yet farmers’ top reason for skipping cover crops is timing: is there still enough fall left after harvest? FieldWise answers that with NASA data. It replays 25 years of NASA POWER daily weather (2001–2025) on the farmer’s field and harvest dates and reports how often each option would have worked, for example “plant cereal rye by Oct 24, it works 9 years in 10.”

From that, it builds a dated 12-month plan, from the cost-share call to the spring kill date, which the farmer can add to their phone calendar. It also checks this week’s forecast for field days and estimates yields with a machine-learning model trained on USDA county yields. For late harvests, it compares drilling rye after harvest with seeding it into the standing crop.

To address “adapting,” it shows how each field’s fall is changing: on our demo field, the safe rye date now comes 5 days earlier than in the early 2000s.

We checked the weather model against USDA’s weekly fieldwork reports (r = 0.74). The result: specific, field-level dates instead of statewide rules of thumb, so more acres are covered over winter.
details:
What it does: FieldWise tells an Ohio farmer the last safe date to plant a cover crop or winter wheat on their own field. It replays 25 years of NASA POWER daily weather (2001–2025) on the farmer’s harvest dates and reports how often each option would have worked: “plant cereal rye by Oct 24, it works 9 years in 10.” It also builds a dated 12-month plan the farmer can add to their phone calendar, turns this week’s forecast into field days, and compares rye seeded into a standing crop with rye drilled after a late harvest. It estimates yields with a machine-learning model and shows how the field’s fall is changing.

Impact: Timing is farmers’ top reason for skipping cover crops, and bare winter soil feeds Lake Erie’s algae blooms. Field-specific dates mean fewer failed seedings and more acres covered.

Validity: Our NASA-based field-day count matches USDA fieldwork reports (r = 0.74).

Tools:

  • Code: Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, JavaScript and Leaflet, hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Data: NASA POWER, GIBS and HLS, plus USDA NASS and SSURGO.
  • AI: Claude helped write the code.

Factors we considered: plain language for farmers, odds instead of promises, crop-insurance rules, and openly reporting what didn’t work: our satellite cover check found no signal yet.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources)
NASA POWER Daily API (point data used for 25-year field histories)
